Geophys. J. R. astr. SOC.( 1979) 59,231-248
Palaeomagne tism of the Fongen-Hyllingen gabbro
complex, southern Scandinavian Caledonides; plate
rotation or polar shift?
N. Abrahamsen, J. R. Wilson, P. Thy, N. 8.O lesen and
K. H. Esbensen Geologisk Znstitut, Aarhus tiniversitet, .&hug, Denmark
Received 1979 February 15; in original form 1978 June 7
Summary. Palaeomagnetic results are presented from the c. 160 km2
Caledonian synorogenic layered Fongen-Hyllingen gabbro complex (of
probable late Silurian age) located about 75 km SE of Trondheim, Norway,
in the allochthonous Seve-Kdli Nappe Complex. A total of 80 oriented
samples from eight sites in the northern part of the gabbro were investigated.
After detailed af demagnetization two stable high coercivity components
emerge: one with a well defined NW direction with D= 325", I= --21°
(ag5= 8", N = 8), and another, less well defined, probably younger, SW
direction with D = 237", I = 6" (ag5= 9', N = 8). Correction for dip of these
two directions gives D = 329", I = - 7" (ag5= 10") and D = 238", I = - I I "
(ag5= 12"), respectively. The corresponding pole positions are P,: 19" N,
225" E and P2:1 9" S, 308" E, respectively. The reversed pole -P2 of the SW
direction lies close to other NW European palaeomagnetic poles of
Caledonian, Upper Silurian-Lower Devonian age. However, the dominant
pole PI is far away from these, and could be due to a late Caledonian geo-
magnetic excursion of considerable duration; or it could record a c. 90"
rotation around a vertical axis of a crustal block within the Scandinavian
Caledonides. Block rotation could have been related to nappe translation,
although geological observations do not at present appear to support the
occurrence of such an event.
1 Introduction
The Fongen-Hyllingen complex is a synorogenic layered gabbro intrusion, situated about
75 km south-east of Trondheim in the Norwegian Caledonides (Fig. 1). A preliminary
account of the complex has been presented by Wilson & Olesen (1975). The present study
has been undertaken to add to the scanty palaeomagnetic results from the Scandinavian
Caledonides.

2 Geology
2.1 REGIONAL SETTING OF THE FONGEN-HYLLINGEN COMPLEX
The Fongen-Hyllingen complex is emplaced in rocks belonging to the allochthonous
Western Complex (e.g. Gee 1975) of the southern Scandinavian Caledonides. The gabbro
intrudes metasediments and metavolcanics of the Fundsjd group, which may correlate with
the Stq5ren group to the west (eg. Roberts, Springer & Wolff 1970), and the Ordovician
(Tremadocian) fossil Dictyonema flabelliforme has been found in rocks of the aureole
(Vogt 1940). The gabbro hornfelsed tightly folded rocks and has inclusions of folded
country rocks, so the intrusion clearly post-dates at least one fold phase. A contact meta-
morphic aureole with index-minerals cordierite, sillimanite and andalusite is developed, with
additional garnet present throughout. The peak of regional metamorphism was reached
shortly after the emplacement of the complex and was accompanied by the main deforma-
tion phase in the area (Olesen et al. 1973). In the western part of the aureole the contact
metamorphic assemblages are overprinted by regional assemblages such as andalusite being
replaced by kyanite and sillimanite by staurolite and white mica.
During regional metamorphism, large parts of the Fongen--Hyllingen complex were
altered to hornblende metagabbros, though often retaining igneous microstructures, and
foliated amplvbolites were produced where metamorphism of the gabbro was accompanied
by penetrative deformation. The gabbro and its envelope were later folded during the
Selbu Tydal phase (Olesen et al. 1973) and the present form of the Fongen-Hyllingen
complex (Wilson & Olesen 1975) is to some extent influenced by its situation in the Tydal
synform which is overturned towards the east. The gabbro can thus with certainty be
regarded as synorogenic.
The Fundsjd Group rocks enveloping the complex occupy a controversial tectono-
stratigraphic position but are interpreted by Zwart (1974) and Gee (1975) as part of the
Kdli (Supergroup) of the Seve --Kdli Nappe complex. Orogenic deformation of this nappe,
with folding, metamorphism and thrusting is considered by Gee & Wilson (1974) to have
both started and finished in Silurian times. Important evidence as to the timing of the end
of the Caledonian orogeny in this region is found at Rdragen, some 50 km SSE of Fongen,
where rocks probably belonging to the Kdli Supergroup are unconformably overlain by
continental conglomerates and sandstones, identified from plant fossils as of Lower
Devonian age (Halle 1916; Hdeg 1936). These Devonian rocks have however been affected
by a late phase of the Caledonian orogeny since they are folded, faulted and show evidence
of low grade metamorphism (Holmsen 1963), and the possibility remains that they were
transported along with the pre-Devonian rocks of the Seve-Kdli Nappe during the final
thrusting.
2.2 PETROLOGY OF THE COMPLEX
Rocks of the Fongen-Hyllingen complex vary from ultramafics, through olivine gabbros,
gabbros and norites to diorites, monzonites and quartz-bearing syenites. Rhythmic layering
is widely developed and there is an extensive cryptic variation (Esbensen, Thy & Wilson
1978). The deepest levels of the intrusion occur in the north where layering is arranged in
a saucer-like form, emphasized by later folding. In the southern part of the complex around
Hyllingen mountain, described by Kisch (1962) and Nilsen (1973), the rhythmic layering
strikes roughly north--south and dips east, the rocks younging consistently to the east.
On the basis of the phase layering and cryptic variation, the complex can be divided into
three parts. These are the Fongen and Ruten sequences in the north (Fig. 1) and the

In the Fongen sequence the lowest cumulates consist of olivine (FO~,)a ccompanied by
chromite. Plagioclase joins olivine roughly when chromite ceases to occur, and these are
accompanied by Ca-rich and Ca-poor pyroxenes higher up. Fe-Ti oxides first crystallize

Ca-poor pyroxenes -t Fe-Ti oxides cumulus assemblage is joined by apatite in the highest
rocks of the Fongen sequence. Cumulus Fe-Ti oxides occur in an average amount of 5 vol.
per cent (range 0-10 per cent) throughout a thickness of some 800 m around and to the
south of the top of Fongen mountain (Fig. 1). These rocks give rise to a major positive
anomaly on the 1 : 50 000 aeromagnetic map of Tydal (Norges Geologiske Undersdkelse,
1721, 111). It is from this area that the major part of the palaeomagnetic sampling was

carried out. The Fongen sequence is overlain by the Ruten sequence in which olivine t
plagioclase + Ca-rich pyroxene cumulates at the base are joined upwards by Ca-poor
pyroxene and then Fe-Ti oxides. The Ruten sequence is considered to represent the
fractionally crystallized products of a new influx of magma after consolidation of the earlier
Fongen sequence.
The southern Hyllingen area represents the upper part of a thick, differentiated gabbroic
sequence and is separated from the northern Fongen-Ruten area by the river Nea valley
where exposures are scanty.
2.3 OPAQUE PHASES FROM THE FONGEN-HY LLINGEN COMPLEX
The primary oxides in the northern part of the complex are titanomagnetite belonging to
the magnetite- ulvospinel solid solution series, and ilmenite belonging to the ilmenite-
haematite solid solution series. Titanomagnetite (30 mol per cent ulvospinel) normally
dominates over ilmenite (0-2 mol per cent haematite). Two microstructural varieties can be
distinguished; ilmenite and titanomagnetite occurring as intercumulus grains interstitial to
silicates, and subhedral to euhedral cumulus grains in which titanomagnetite dominates
over ilmenite. The grain size of the cumulus Fe-Ti oxides ranges from 1 mm to below
0.05 mm.
Two types of titanomagnetite are found, the first indicating an early stage of ulvospinel
exsolution and the second a sub-solidus oxidation of ulvospinel at high temperature during
magmatic or late-magmatic conditions (Buddington & Lindsley 1964). Ulvospinel can be
completely or partly replaced by magnetite/ilmenite intergrowth and is found in one third
of the samples where it occurs in a fine cloth-like microstructure with possible single or
pseudosingle domain magnetite in the micron-range. The most common microstructures are,
however, a subhedral coarse ilmenite/magnetite intergrowth or an intergrowth of fine
ilmenite lamellae in magnetite corresponding to oxidation class 11-111 (Ade-Hall et al. 1968).
Similar assemblages have been described, among others by Vincent (1960) and Mathison
(1975). Fine acicular Al- Fe spinel is found in the magnetite and, as proposed by Turnock
& Eugster (1 962), results from exsolution.
Ilmenite occurs as mm-sized interstitial grains, sometimes with tapering twins. Ilmenite
can replace titanomagnetite when they have mutual grain boundaries. Equivalent micro-
structures have been interpreted as resulting from replacement during crystallization (Gierth
& Krause 1973) or as a sub-solidus reaction (Krause & Pape 1975). Haematite exsolution
is not observed, which according to Ramdohr (1969) indicates less than 6 per cent Fe203
in the ilmenite-haematite solid solution series.
Sulphides occur in amounts less than 2 per cent of the total opaque phase in the cumulus
magnetite zone. Pyrrhotite is the dominant sulphide and may contribute to the remanence
in a few cases. It occurs in interstitial to subhedral aggregates with minor amounts of pent-
landite and chalcopyrite with sub-solidus exsolution microstructures.
Secondary magnetite, and to a lesser extent ilmenite, is formed during late-magmatic
replacement of olivine with magnetite- orthopyroxene symplectites or by reactions between
olivine and plagioclase. The magnetite occurs with the silicates in a vermicular to tabular
symplectic intergrowth or as irregular grains from a few microns to mm-size often surround-
ing partly or completely altered olivine. Magnetite and ilmenite are also found as tabular
to acicular grains along the prismatic cleavage in the pyroxenes. Magnetite is only altered to
a relatively minor degree with a weak marginal decomposition to goethte in some instances.
The opaque phases hence record a prolonged crystallization and sub-solidus re-equilibra-
tion history. The ilmenite/magnetite intergrowth clearly post-dates the ulvospinel/magnetite

intergrowth, and is interpreted as a sub-solidus oxidation from ulvospinel (Buddington &
Lindsley 1964) which occurred during or after the metamorphism. The exsolution of Al-Fe
spinel post-dates the ulvospinel exsolution. The oxides derived from silicates are considered
to be a synantectic result of magmatic cooling at elevated temperature (Esbensen 1978),
as well as a result of late magmatic interactions, as described by Ambler & Ashly (1977).
The sulphides show susceptibility to low temperature re-equilibration during or after the
oxidation of ulvospinel to ilmenite.
3 Palaeomagnetic investigations
A total of 1 11 palaeomagnetic samples were collected from eight sites in the gabbro around
Fongen mountain (Fig. 1, sites 1-7 and 1 l), two sites in strongly deformed and amphiboli-
tized gabbro (sites 8 and 9) and one site in a trondhjemite intrusion (site 10).
In the field 10 hand samples were collected from each site with an areal coverage of
typically 30 x 100 m2. Unmetamorphosed sites were selected from previous knowledge.
Unweathered hand samples were loosened by a hammer, the north direction was measured
by means of a magnetic compass and marked on a horizontal surface of plaster of Paris.
The compass measurements were individually controlled by topographical sights and no
significant discrepancies were encountered. The strike and dip of the strata were further
measured in 10 places at each site, and the palaeomagnetic site mean directions (Table 1)
were also later corrected for the initial dip (see below); the mean errors of the mean dip and
strike are estimated to be about ? 1" and ? 2" respectively.
In the laboratory several 1-in. oriented cores were drilled from each sample, and a total of
379 1 x 1-in. specimens were thus obtained, 302 being from the gabbro proper. The palaeo-
magnetic results from the amphibolites (sites 8 and 9) and the trondhjemite (site 10) were
extremely scattered, and are not considered further.
The geometrical mean of the volume susceptibility of the gabbro measured partly on
hand samples (1 1) and partly on cored specimens (14) was 2 x lOW3G/Oe(r ange 3.0-400 x
and the mean of the respective Q-values was 2 (range 0.4-10). The natural remanent
magnetization (NRM) of all the specimens was initially measured using a Digico spinner
magnetometer. The direction of the mean NRM of the gabbro was D = 327", I = 64" (ag5=
5.2', N= 302 specimens), which is fairly close to the present geomagnetic field (Do= 356",
I - 75') as well as the axial dipole field (Do=O' , Io= 75.8'). A dominating viscous
remanent magnetic component is therefore present as a recent overprint. The intensity of
the NRM varied 4 orders of magnitude (range 1.6 x lo-' to 1.4 x lo-' emulcc) with the geo-
metrical mean within the sites ranging between 0.3 x and 4.5 x lO-'emu/cc, and with an
overall geometrical mean of 2 x emulcc, N = 302. After some pilot demagnetizations,
one specimen from each hand sample was stepwise af demagnetized in zero field (? 107)
to peak fields of 50,100,200,300,400 and 600 Oe. In several cases this range was extended
up to about 1800 Oe and occasionally supplemented by demagnetization data from another
specimen from the same sample. Typical intensity decay curves are shown in Fig. 2.
The median destructive fields (mdf) of the specimens were typically between 50 and
200 Oe (65 per cent of the specimens), whereas the mdf for 10 per cent of the specimens
was below 50 Oe and for 10 per cent above 600 Oe. No correlation between the mdf and the
intensity of NRM was found.
The major carriers of the NRM are titanomagnetite and the high coercivity components
of the remanent magnetization are probably due to fine grained single or pseudo-single
domain titanomagnetites, which may be present as the cumulus/intercumulus phase and/or
as secondary alteration products of the mafic minerals. Two samples (1 1.21 and 12.21 from

Palaeomagnetism of Fongen Hyllingen complex 239
~
During the af demagnetizations (Fig. 3) the direction of the RM of the eight gabbro sites
converged and in most cases stabilized in a characteristic up-dip NW-direction with a well
defined site mean of D = 325", I = - 2 1" (ag5= 8" ,N = 8) which becomes 329" , - 7" (ag5=
lo", ct Table 1) when applying dip correction (i.e. rotating the layering to a horizontal
position).
Site 1, however, behaves in a different way. It converges against a subhorizontal SW-
direction, and when taking a closer look at the demagnetization stereograms of the other
gabbro sites, it appears that a characteristic SW-component is present in all the other sites,
although not as clearly depicted as in site 1 which only sporadically shows the NW-direction
(except specimens 8 and 10, Fig. 3).
The SW-direction is obviously not as well defined as the NW-direction, and a formal
palaeomagnetic stability index such as that of Symons & Stupavsky (1974), which applies
well for the NW-direction is of but little help in defining the SW-direction. In 17 cases the
SW-component is revealed in or even dominates the NRM, and the remanence migrates to
the NW during progressive af cleaning. In some cases the SW-component emerges in a
moderate demagnetizing field between 200 and lOOOOe, but stable high coercivity SW-
components are only found in a few cases, notably in site 6. The coercivity spectra of the
NW- and the SW-components apparently overlap, and both cover a wide range, probably
reflecting the wide range in grain size of the magnetic phases present.
The best evidence for the relative magnetic chronology is seen in sites 3,4 and 7 (Fig. 3),
where the SW-component is clearly removed by cleaning in higher ac fields, thus illustrating
the dominance of the high coercivity components of the NW-direction. In site 4 younger
viscous components are nearly absent, making the picture even more clear. In this site, it
also appears that the blocking period of the magnetic recordings was of sufficient duration
to capture normal as well as reverse polarity of both directions.
As all the petrological events of relevance to the magnetic blocking of the remanence
occurred below the respective Curie-points (G 575°C for titanomagnetite), the magnetizing
processes must have occurred during the postmagmatic and metamorphic (and tectonic)
history of the gabbro.
Further, the local temperature of the gabbro during the blocking of the SW-component
was not higher than the blocking temperatures of the NW-component, otherwise the NW-
direction could not have been preserved; both remanences appear to be carried essentially
by titanomagnetites of equivalent Curie-points. The generally higher coercivities of the NW-
component probably also indicate that at least part of the carriers of the NW-component
are more fine-grained than those of the SE-component.
Finally, it should be noted that in site 1 only, five specimens (Fl-5) have relatively high
content of pyrrhotite as compared to magnetite; the Curie-point of pyrrhotite is fairly low
(300-325"C), and site 1 is the only one in which the SW-component is completely
dominant. This supports the other indications that the SW-component is younger than the
NW-component
,
Considering the change in direction from the SW- to the NW-quadrant shown by the
thermally demagnetized specimens (Fig. 2), we conclude that the SW-direction was most
likely acquired at lower temperatures (below about 45OoC, Fig. 2) than the high coercivity
NW-component, and is likely to be a younger magnetization, although high coercivity phases
are also present.
Correlating the genesis of specific opaque phases with the two characteristic remanent
directions, however, is not easy in spite of detailed information from polished sections and
magnetic properties. No clear correlation with any specific phase or degree of oxidation has
been noted, except the mentioned correlation at site 1 between pyrrhotite and the SW-

component, and a tendency for the NW-component to correlate with high temperature
secondary magnetite in the mafic phases together with the cloth-like microstructures of the
ulvospinel-magnetite intergrowth. This may account for part of the high coercivity
components most likely due to single/pseudosingle domain grains, and may suggest that the
high coercivity part of the NW-component was induced before the oxidation of ulvospinel,
the SW-component being still younger.
In Table 1 the site mean values of the SW-components present are summarized. The site
mean of the SW-direction is found to be D = 237", I= 6" (ag5= 9", N= 8) without dip
correction, and D = 238", I= - 11" (ag5= 12") with dip correction applied. The precision
parameter is generally lower for the SW- than for the NW-component.
4 Discussion of the palaeomagnetic data
In Fig. 4 the two mean directions of Table 1 are plotted in stereographic projection before
and after dip correction, and it is seen that they are very nearly orthogonal to each other.
Correction for dip does not improve the scatter of either direction; actually ag5is slightly
increased (by about 12 per cent) in both cases. The change in mean direction is only 14 and
17" for the NW- and SW-directions respectively and only the inclination is essentially
affected. The initial dip of the rhythmic layering before deformation is unknown; a qualified

SW components. Triangles are dip corrected directions, dots and circles are in situ directions (without dip
correction). The circles of 95 per cent confidence are shown for the site means, ag5b eing slightly greater
for the dip corrected ones.

guess may be somewhere between 0 and 10" away from the margins of the intrusion, that is
very roughly in the present down-dip direction for the sites shown in Fig. 1. The present
dip of the sites (Table 1) varies between 20 and 30" and if dip correction must be applied,
the true remanent mean values may be expected to fall somewhere between the dip
corrected and non-dip corrected values. Whether or not the values should be corrected for
dip will be discussed later.
The apparent palaeomagnetic pole positions PI and Pz, corresponding to the NW- and
SW-direction, respectively, are 11" N, 227" E and 11" S, 312" E before dip correction;
19" N, 225"E and 19"S, 308" E after dip correction (Table 1); the geographical mean
coordinates of the gabbro sites are 63.1"N71 1.6"E. In Fig. 5 the two poles, with and
without dip correction, are plotted together with other palaeozoic poles of NW-Europe
as compiled in Table 2.
Figure 5. Apparent palaeomagnetic pole positions for NW-European Late-Precambrian and Palaeozoic
poles as compiled in Table 2, the open symbols are reversed (Lambert zenithal equal area projection).
The Late-Precambrian apparent polar wander curve as indicated with a broken arrow is not yet well
defined, although a rapid shift is likely to have occurred somewhere in between Late Sveconorwegian
(-800 Myr) and Lower Ordovician time (e.g. Abrahamsen 1977; Patchett & Bylund 1977). Other
apparent shifts as indicated roughly by arrows are between the clusters of Ordovician-Silurian, Silurian-
Devonian, Devonian-Upper Carboniferous and Upper Carboniferous-Permian poles. The data for Lower
Palaeozoic poles for the British Islands are somewhat scattered. Significant experimental errors are
unlikely; the scatter of results reflects polar movements during this interval, differential strike slip
movements and differences on either side of the Iapetus suture. The apparent pole position P, of the NW
direction of the Fongen Gabbro (with and without dip correction and with 95 per cent oval of confidence
indicated) is situated between several Late-Precambri-an poles, and may be interpreted either as a polar
migration of some 50-60" with a duration of at least 10"yr in Upper Silurian-Lower Devonian, or as a
horizontal block rotation of some 60-90' anticlockwise (or some 90-120" clockwise) after the primary
magnetic imprint of the NW direction. The apparent pole position -P2o f the reversed SW direction, being
some 10-20" and 25-30" away from the Silurian and Devonian clusterings of poles respectively, may
accordingly be interpreted as due to a secondary magnetization, imposed during final cooling after the
regional Caledonian metamorphism and nappe translations. In this 'Case the in siru pole - P, (without dip
correction) should apply, and again the deviation may either be interpreted in terms of a minor polar
migration or possibly a clockwise rotation of some 10-20" after the magnetic imprint of the SW
direction.

### page_14
244 N. Abrahamsen et al.
As a first approximation, the pole - P2, corresponding to a reversed SW-direction, may
readily be interpreted as a reversely polarized palaeomagnetic pole of Caledonian, Upper
Silurian-Lower Devonian age, as it is not far away from other known poles of this age (see
further discussion below).
The position of the pole PI of the NW-direction corresponding to the dominant NW
magnetization of the gabbro is, however, not readily explained. It is situated about 90"
away from the P2 pole, and is placed in the NE-Pacific area (Fig. 5). The pole PI cannot be
explained as a much younger magnetization because of the absence of any correlation with
post-Palaeozoic poles, bearing in mind the dominant nature of the PI pole over the Pz pole
and their apparent relative age.
As components of both polarities appear to be present in some specimens (notably 22.3,
24.31, 31,32, 38, 41.2, 42.2, 52.2, 58, 68.21, 105.21 and 107) it could be argued that the
NW-direction is just the accidental mean of two shallow SW-subcomponents of opposite
polarity (SW and NE) combining to a NW-direction, possibly supplied by a steep normal
component of a recently induced viscous component. This is quite unlikely, because the
convergence of the NW-direction is so well pronounced (it would be expected to show
a random variation confined to the vertical plane orthogonal to the SW-NE axis) and
because the recent viscous remanent magnetization, if not completely destroyed by the
cleaning process, would tend to parallelize the combined directions in a steep northerly
downdip (or southerly updip in case of a reversed field) direction in the vertical plane
containing the SW-direction.
It would therefore appear that both poles must be explained in a Palaeozoic context.
One possibility is that the PI pole could be an original Silurian/Devonian TCRM, the
apparent palaeomagnetic field having made an excursion of about 90" to the pole PI in Late
Caledonian time, which was stable long enough to cause the NW-direction to be locked in
firmly at the expense of the (probably slightly younger) P2 pole of the general Caledonian
SW direction. Considering the dimensions of the gabbro, the depth of emplacement (15-
20 km) and particularly the synorogenic environment, the total cooling time of the gabbro
to below the active blocking range of the TRM, of which the thermomagnetic blocking range
is a considerable part, must have been of the order of several millions of years (e.g. Jaeger
1968). This palaeomagnetic polar excursion explanation is not very plausible, as out of
about 50 published palaeomagnetic investigations of NW-European Palaeozoic formations
(e.g. Creer 1970; McElhinny 1973) there are only two poles in the vicinity ofPl. These are
Nos. 3 and 9 in Table 2, both of which are too old and with a high scatter (ag5= 20°), the
palaeomagnetic reliability of No. 3 in addition being questionable (McElhinny 1973, note
p. 289). The Late Ordovician (Caradocian) probably non-axial dipole field, which appears
to have been recorded by some hypabyssal intrusions in North Wales and in dyke swarms in
northern England (Piper, private communication, 1978) is also too old for our case.
Another interesting possibility is that the two directions record the rotation of a block
within the Scandinavian Caledonides. A block including the Fongen-Hyllingen complex
must then be supposed to have rotated anticlockwise around a subvertical axis by an angle
of about 90' relative to the normal NE or NNE updip Palaeozoic field direction after cooling
down below the effective blocking temperatures (say c. 500-550°C) of the titano-
magnetites present. This rotation could presumably have taken place during the nappe
emplacements. During or shortly after the rotation, and after a reversal of the field polarity
(both polarities are known from other investigations of Caledonian rocks), the SW-direction
was then induced as a secondary TCRM, which now defines the 'Caldeonian' pole Pz of the
gabbro complex. As the -P2 pole lies some 10-20" W of the main cluster of other Upper
Silurian-Lower Devonian poles (Fig. 9, it could be postulated that this direction was
Downloaded

### page_15
Palaeomagnetism of Fongen -Hyllingen complex 245
locked in prior to another possible 10-20" final clockwise rotation before the end of nappe
emplacement.
According to this hypothesis the dominant NW direction does not define a true palaeo-
magnetic pole but rather the local rotation of the pertinent block. Rotation in the opposite
(clockwise) direction of about 90' is an equally possible alternative; in this case no reversal
needs to have taken place between the two recording times.
it would be useful to try to relate the possible timing of the acquisition of the two
magnetic components to the geological events in which the Fongen-Hyllingen complex
has been involved. Contact metamorphic assemblages surrounding the complex indicate
emplacement at about 5 Kb, equivalent to a depth of 15-20km, and intrusion was shortly
followed by the peak of regional metamorphism at up to about 7 Kb and 650°C (Olesen
et al. 1973). In view of the well defined nature of the NW-direction and the high tempera-
tures involved during regional metamorphism, it seems likely that this magnetic component
was established during cooling after the regional metamorphic peak. Broadly speaking the
peak of regional metamorphism and deformation was followed by two phases of mesoscopic
folding (Olesen et al. 1973), which appear to have had little effect on the competent gabbro
complex. These were followed by a major fold phase, the Selbu-Tydal phase of Olesen et al.
(1973) which influenced the shape of the gabbro complex (Wilson & Olesen 1975) and had
the effect of steepening the dips of the rhythmic layering around Fongen mountain where
most of the palaeomagnetic samples were collected. This Selgu-Tydal phase comprises
essentially open folds with no associated axial plane foliation. The temperatures prevailing
during this fold episode are poorly known, and it is not clear whether the NW and/or the SW
components pre- or post-date this fold phase and should consequently be corrected for dip.
The closest and hence most relevant palaeomagnetic results from Scandinavia at present
available are from the upper Ordovician synorogenic Sulitjelma Gabbro some 500 km to the
NNE (pole 11 in Fig. 5), from the Upper Silurian Ringerike Sandstone 350 km to the south
(pole 19), from the Lower or Middle Devonian sediments at Roragen 50 km to the south
(pole 22), and from the Middle Devonian Kvamshesten Sandstone some 350 km to the
south-west (pole 23).
The palaeomagnetic pole from the (older) Sulitjelma Gabbro, when uncorrected for dip,
is in good agreement with those from the British Isles (poles 6--lO), and the Sulitjelma pole
clearly lies outside any block possibly involved in only a 'local' rotation in the southern
Scandinavian Caledonides. The precision of pole 11, however, is quite low (k = 6, ag5=
28", N= 6), the sites sampled being metamorphosed, tectonized and folded (Piper 1974,
1975a; Mason 1975), and the constraints from this pole on possible rotational interpreta-
tions hence would be rather broad.
The Devonian Roragen Old Red Sandstones (pole 22) are late orogenic; deposited on rocks
of the nappe which contains the Fongen--Hyllingen complex; they may therefore post-date
the possible rotational movements of the block containing the gabbro. The palaeomagnetic
poles for the Roragen Sandstone, the Ringerike Sandstone (pole 19) and the Kvamshesten
Sandstone (pole 23) are mutually consistent and define an 'Old Red' Norwegian pole close
to 20" N, 160" E. A moderate rotation of 15" anticlockwise for the Kvamshesten area was
suggested by Storetvedt (1967), because of the unconformity and slightly younger age of the
sediments as compared to the base, to make a better coincidence of the Norwegian Old Red
poles. Considering the Fisher statistics of pole 23 (ags= 9"), however, a rotation of only a
few degrees may suffice in this case. The poles of four supposed Palaeozoic dykes on the
island of Bornholm (pole 16) are also close to this Devonian Old Red pole. The Roragen
pole position therefore appears to have been established essentially after the suggested
rotation of the pertinent block containing the Fongen -Hyllingen complex.

### page_16
246 N. Abrahamsen et al.
5 Conclusions
In the Fongen -Hyllingen gabbro complex two characteristic palaeomagnetic directions are
recorded, a well defined NW direction (P,)a nd a less well defined but distinct SW direction
(Pz), and it appears that the NW component predates the SW one. The -Pz pole of the SW
(reversed) direction lies fairly close to late Caledonian poles from Scandinavia. It seems that
the PI pole was established during cooling after the peak of regional metamorphism and may
record either a persistent geomagnetic excursion during Late Caledonian time, or a roughly
90" rotation of a crustal block in the Scandinavian Caledonides.
In the last decade numerous palaeomagnetic investigations have been published,
suggesting azimuthal block rotations of crustal segments of local to regional scales in
orogenic collision zones. In most cases the field geologist had no observations to corroborate
such ideas prior to the palaeomagnetic evidence. Some minor or medium scale examples in
the Mediterranean mobile belt are the Northern Calcareous Alps showing about 45" clock-
wise rotation with respect to Eurasia since the Jurassic (Mauritsch & Frisch 1978), the
Corso-Sardinian Plate showing about 50' anticlockwise rotation during the Early Miocene
(De Jong et al. 1973; Storetvedt & Markhus 1978), and the Iberian and Italian peninsulae
also showing anticlockwise rotations of between 35 and 70" since the Triassic. These and
other examples from Turkey and Japan are summarized by McElhinny (1973).
Probably the most detailed sampled Palaeozoic region is the British Isles, the older
Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic data of which are known to be quite complex. During the
Caledonian orogeny the isles appear to have behaved as a separate crustal plate (Piper 1978),
and in a recent palaeocontinental reconstruction Morel & Irving (1978), although with some
hesitation, suggest that between 450 and -400 Ma the British Isles (perhaps in part)
-
rotated over 90' relative to Gondwanaland about a local axis. The Fongen- Hyllingen
gabbro complex may have recorded the rotation of a comparable orogenic plate within the
Scandinavian Caledonides.
Other apparently anomalous Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic results from Europe have been
reported, such as two Irish palaeomagnetic directions from the Mid-Ordovician Mweelrea
ignimbrites and the Connemara gabbros (Morris et al. 1973) which may be interpreted either
as 40' anticlockwise and clockwise local rotations, respectively, or as geomagnetic
excursions. It is hardly possible at this stage definitively to decide which hypothesis
--
geomagnetic excursion or block rotation -is to be preferred to account for the palaeo-
magnetic results from the Fongen-Hyllingen complex. Further palaeomagnetic investiga-
tions from the Scandinavian Caledonides, as well as structural evidence related to possible
azimuthal rotation, may throw more light on this interesting problem.
Acknowledgments
Financial support from the Danish Natural Science Research Council and the Carlsbergfond
of Denmark is gratefully acknowledged. The help of Lars Lukassen in the field and with
sample preparations, and that of Inger S. Jensen, Lars NQrgaard Jensen and Anders Rehkopff
with measurements, is gratefully acknowledged. Some of the susceptibility measurements
were made possible by G. Schonharting, Copenhagen. We wish to thank J. D. A. Piper for
helpful advice and criticism, and K. M. Creer for his constructive comments on the manu-
script.
